name: Medicinal clay

card.summary: Fine natural clays such as bentonite, kaolin and fuller's earth applied as masks to absorb skin oil and tighten the look of pores, or traditionally taken by mouth.
card.aka: healing clay, bentonite, kaolin, fuller's earth
card.note: Clay sold for eating may carry heavy-metal contamination; quality varies.

quick.overview:
Medicinal clays are natural clay minerals, mainly smectites such as montmorillonite (the main component of bentonite) and kaolins, used on the skin and traditionally swallowed. For looks, clay masks are used to soak up oil and give a matte, clean-pored complexion.

Human research mostly concerns oral smectite for diarrhoea; laboratory work has found some clays kill bacteria in vitro. Skin-appearance claims rest on traditional use and cosmetic practice.
quick.how: As a cosmetic, clay is mixed with water or sold ready-made as a paste mask, left on the face for a short period and rinsed off, usually for oily or breakout-prone skin. Traditional systems such as Persian medicine and Andean practice also used clays internally.
quick.risks: Clays can contain heavy metals such as arsenic, lead and cadmium, a main concern raised for medicinal use [1]. Masks can irritate skin and are not for the eye area. Edible clay is not a regulated food in many places.

lead: Medicinal clays are fine-grained phyllosilicate minerals, including smectites (such as montmorillonite in bentonite) and kaolins, valued for absorbing water, oils and ions [2]. Pliny the Elder and Aristotle wrote of healing earths, and clays have been eaten or applied to the skin across many cultures [2][3].

In appearance care they appear mainly as face and hair masks. Fuller's earth, named for workers who cleaned wool, is described as removing oil and dirt from skin and hair, and in India multani mitti is widely used in cosmetics [4]. Clay masks are generally suited to oily skin and deep cleansing of pores [5].

Research covers several areas: a Cochrane review examined smectite as an add-on for acute infectious diarrhoea in children [6]; a laboratory study found that some hydrated clays are bactericidal because of soluble Fe(2+) and Al(3+) [7]; and studies of Armenian bole and other historical clays examine composition and heavy-metal content [3][8].

chain: Clay mask absorbs surface oil and dirt
Skin looks matte with cleaner-looking pores
angle.text: A clay mask is rinsed off after a short time and leaves skin feeling less oily; the effect is on surface oil rather than pore size itself. Some traditional systems also claim antibacterial and detoxifying effects.

infobox: Bentonite, kaolin, fuller's earth, Armenian bole

paras: Cosmetic use centres on masks. Ancient Egyptians used facial masks and Ayurvedic practice combined herbs with clays; the first US facial mask patent dates to 1875 [5]. Fuller's earth is also sold as a cleaning clay for skin and hair [4].
The Andean 'chaco' is an edible clay used with water for digestive discomfort [9]. Traditional Persian medicine recorded many medicinal clays [10].

Heavy-metal toxicity (including arsenic, cadmium, lead, nickel) is a main limitation of medicinal clay, and traditional treatments of Armenian bole have been studied to reduce it [8]. Some masks can irritate skin [5].

A Cochrane review assessed smectite as a complementary treatment for acute infectious diarrhoea in children [6]. Laboratory research shows certain clays kill pathogens when hydrated, via soluble iron and aluminium [7]. No trials of clay masks for pores or oily skin were identified in the available literature.

timeline.event: First US facial mask patent granted in Ohio[5]
